item.title: Symmetry-preserving quantum compilation
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Measurement-assisted and LCU Clifford+T compilation synthesizes continuous time evolution while preserving exact continuous symmetries such as SU(2), reducing the required T-count by approximately a factor of five compared to standard symmetry-agnostic compilation for estimating 1D Heisenberg transport exponents.

Grade 0.432 · 2.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Theory of Trotter Error with Commutator Scaling” · Maryam Mudassar, Zhi-Yuan Wei, Alexander Schuckert, Michael J. Lawler, Michael J. Gullans, Daniel Gottesman

Figure

Transport scaling comparison showing transferred magnetization versus time steps. For matched dynamical transport exponent accuracy (1/z≈2/3), the symmetry-preserving LCU compilation reduces the cumulative T-count compared to standard synthesis and BRS axial synthesis.

Asks

How can continuous symmetry-preserving time evolutions be compiled into fault-tolerant discrete gate sets without introducing symmetry-breaking synthesis errors?

Before

Standard symmetry-agnostic synthesis (such as gridsynth/Solovay-Kitaev) introduces off-axis transverse errors that break continuous conservation laws and yielded incorrect transport exponents at 54 T gates per two-site Trotter step.

But

Demonstrated for spin-1/2 systems with exact SU(2) symmetry, 1D lattice gauge theories, and fermionic models (Fermi-Hubbard, electronic structure); higher-spin systems remain unexplored.

Tools

Measurement and feed-forward · Linear combination of unitaries (LCU) · Repeat-until-success (RUS) axial compilation · Jordan–Wigner transformation

Abstract

Fault-tolerant quantum simulation requires compiling symmetry-preserving time evolutions into discrete gate sets. Standard Clifford+T synthesis can break continuous symmetries even when the target evolution preserves them, causing compiled simulations to lose essential features of the original system. We develop a fault-tolerant compilation framework that preserves SU(2) symmetry exactly. We characterize the number-theoretic obstruction preventing symmetry-preserving unitary Clifford+T circuits from approximating arbitrary SU(2)-symmetric evolutions and circumvent it using measurement and feed-forward. The resulting synthesis confines compilation errors to the symmetry-preserving operator algebra rather than introducing symmetry-breaking perturbations. We demonstrate the algorithm by simulating transport in the one-dimensional Heisenberg model. At a lower matched T-count, for instance, 54 T gates per two-site Trotter step, standard synthesis yields an incorrect transport exponent, whereas our symmetry-preserving compilation reproduces the expected exponent for the same expected T-count. If instead each approach is allocated whatever resources are necessary to estimate this exponent to the same accuracy, our construction reduces the T-count by approximately a factor of five. We further extend the framework to gauge symmetries in lattice gauge theories and to particle-number and spin symmetries in fermionic models relevant to quantum chemistry and the Fermi-Hubbard model. These results show that symmetry-preserving fault-tolerant compilation can qualitatively change the effects of synthesis error while substantially reducing the resources required for quantum simulation.

item.title: Beyond Pure Dephasing: Quantum Error Correction in Single Molecules Requires Multiple Spins
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Two-level error-correcting encoding combines embedded dephasing correction in S−𝓈 molecular spin dimers with an outer multi-qubit code, bypassing the loss of transferred coherence in anharmonic qudits.

Grade 0.377 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Matteo Mezzadri, Silvia Macedonio, Luca Lepori, Emilio Macaluso, Francesco Albarelli, Richard E. P. Winpenny, Alessandro Chiesa, Stefano Carretta1

Figure

Entanglement infidelity Perr of planar logical rotations versus dephasing time T2 for embedded S=3/2 and S=7/2 units at different relaxation times T1, compared against bare spin-1/2 qubits.

Asks

How can fault-tolerant quantum error correction handle both diagonal dephasing and off-diagonal relaxation errors in single-molecule spin architectures?

But

Simulated under Markovian secular spin-bath dynamics at Bz=0.35 T; assumes ideal syndrome measurement and two-qubit gates on the outer code; inter-molecule entanglement mechanisms not implemented.

Tools

Redfield master equation · Knill–Laflamme conditions · Pauli twirling approximation · Steane [[7,1,3]] code · Star-shaped multi-spin clusters

Abstract

We propose multi-spin molecules as a viable architecture for fault-tolerant quantum computing. To this aim, we introduce a correction protocol handling both diagonal and off-diagonal errors, typically associated with dephasing and relaxation. The scheme is based on a hybrid encoding which combines dephasing-tolerant units suppressing the leading pure dephasing error into a multi-spin molecule implementing a multi-qubit code for residual off-diagonal errors. Our proposal leverages peculiar properties of molecular spins, i.e. the strong hierarchy between different errors and the possibility to engineer multi-spin molecules at the synthetic level. Moreover, it addresses the important issue of the loss of coherences in anharmonic systems subject to off-diagonal errors, which hampers their correction at the single spin level. Thanks to the huge suppression of dephasing by the first-level code, we numerically demonstrate the potential performance of this strategy even with a limited number of spins per logical unit.

item.title: Quantum simulation of field-tunable spin spectroscopy of the quantum magnet Cs2CoCl4 on a trapped-ion quantum computer
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Dynamic spin structure factor and quantum Fisher information density of 36-site Cs2CoCl4 chain simulated on 36-qubit quantum processor with 420 two-qubit gates per state. Error-mitigated spectra achieve Pearson correlation and structural similarity >0.9 against DMRG-CV and Pearson correlation >0.85 against inelastic neutron scattering.

Grade 0.370 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Elias Kokkas, Nora Bauer, Justin Provazza, Mark E. Nowakowski, Kathleen Hamilton, Gilles Buchs, Andrew Sornborger, Travis S. Humble, Ananth Kaushik, Martin Roetteler

Figure

Longitudinal (Szz), transverse (Sxx), and total (Stot) dynamical structure factors plotted as frequency ω/J against momentum q/π across four transverse fields hx/J∈{0,0.764,1.146,1.604}, comparing DMRG-CV, DMRG+Trotter, and error-mitigated hardware measurements.

Asks

How much reliable magnetic spectral information and field evolution can be recovered from noisy quantum processors under aggressive circuit compression?

But

Zero temperature target, open boundary conditions on 36 sites with evolution restricted to 20 Trotter steps (Jt=12). State preparation fidelity averaged over spin channels is >0.6.

Tools

IonQ Forte Enterprise 36-qubit processor · Variational circuit compression · Ancilla-free local kick protocol · Correction-vector DMRG (DMRG-CV) · Error mitigation

Abstract

The collective excitation spectra of quantum magnets provide a direct test of quantum computers as tools for studying strongly correlated matter. Hardware noise limits the circuit depths available for these calculations, leaving the question of how much magnetic information can survive circuit compression. Using IonQ's 36 qubit Forte Enterprise processor, we simulate the magnetic excitation spectra and spin dynamics of a 36 site Heisenberg XXZ chain describing the quantum magnet Cs2CoCl4 in a transverse field using quantum circuits containing just 420 two qubit gates. The workflow combines an ancilla free local kick protocol with classical tensor network compression, encoding both ground state preparation and time evolution. The reconstructed dynamical structure factors capture the evolution from a broad two spinon continuum toward a dispersive branch with magnon character near the expected critical field. We observe an interesting field driven sign reversal of the nearest neighbor spin correlations which shows a complementary signature of this magnetic evolution. Our error mitigation methods bring the reconstructed total spectra into close agreement with density matrix renormalization group calculations, with Pearson correlation and structural similarity above 0.9 and normalized mean squared error below 0.15. We also perform comparisons with experimental inelastic neutron scattering measurements to connect the recovered excitations to the material's magnetic response. Our results demonstrate that circuit compression and error mitigation allow noisy quantum processors to recover both collective excitations and local magnetic correlations providing a quantitative benchmark for quantum spectroscopy and a basis for extending these methods to more complex magnetic systems.

item.title: Quasiparticle quantum simulation of materials with the Bethe-Salpeter equation
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Compiling multi-excitonic Bethe-Salpeter equation Hamiltonians into first-quantized block encodings requires O~(N) Toffolis and O(log⁡N) logical qubits, or O~(N) Toffolis and O~(N) qubits. Triexciton eigenvalue estimation in ∼103-atom semiconductors reduces Toffoli counts by 106–107 relative to full-Hamiltonian quantum simulation.

Grade 0.369 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Jielun Chen, Jiace Sun, Garnet Kin-Lic Chan

Figure

Toffoli and logical qubit counts vs k-point mesh size Nk for diamond triexciton (m=3) eigenvalue estimation at 0.1 eV precision, comparing full-Hamiltonian simulation methods with BSE implementations.

Asks

Can quantum simulation of material excited states be made computationally practical on fault-tolerant hardware by operating within a classical quasiparticle Bethe-Salpeter equation framework rather than simulating the full electronic Hamiltonian?

Before

Full-Hamiltonian quantum simulation of a 10×10×10 diamond mesh required 3.7×1017 Toffolis in second quantization (THC) and 4.2×1018 Toffolis in first quantization (plane waves).

But

Heuristic GW/Bethe-Salpeter equation framework with static screened interaction and Tamm-Dancoff approximation; fixed quasiparticle count mtot=2m.

Tools

First-quantized orbital-based block encoding · Tensor hypercontraction (THC) integral factorization · Qubitization · Space-group symmetry adaptation

Abstract

The first-principles quantum simulation of the full electronic Hamiltonian of a material model of realistic size appears daunting even in a future era of fully fault-tolerant quantum computers. In contrast, classical simulations of material excited states rely on heuristic quasiparticle frameworks, such as the GW approximation and Bethe-Salpeter equation, where only a few quasiparticles are explicitly considered. Here we give a detailed description of quasiparticle quantum simulation for multi-excitonic states within the BSE. We develop an explicit first-quantized, orbital-based block encoding of the multi-exciton BSE Hamiltonian for qubitization, and reduce its cost using integral factorization and crystal symmetries. For a materials model of size N, and a fixed number of quasiparticles, the resulting algorithms require widetildeO(N) Toffoli gates and O(logN) logical qubits, or, using space-time tradeoffs, widetildeO(√N) Toffoli gates and widetildeO(√N) logical qubits, achieving up to a sixth power reduction in Toffoli count, or up to exponential reduction in qubit count, versus standard full Hamiltonian simulation techniques that have been explored in materials simulation. Resource estimates for the classically challenging problem of triexcitonic eigenvalue estimation across a range of semiconductor models of a realistic physical size of O(10³) atoms, show that our Toffoli-optimized implementation reduces the Toffoli count by 10⁶-10⁷ relative to full Hamiltonian simulation estimates, while a qubit-optimized implementation requires only a few hundred logical qubits. More broadly, these results show that classical heuristic frameworks will be essential in the design of future fault-tolerant quantum algorithms for materials.

item.title: Ordering-Aware Theory of Trotter Error
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Constructed efficiently computable, ordering-sensitive finite-step Trotter error bounds for arbitrarily high-order product formulas on geometrically local Hamiltonians. For product formulas of order p>2, bounds improve on previous analytical bounds by several orders of magnitude and overestimate actual error by only 40%−50%.

Grade 0.357 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Theory of Trotter Error with Commutator Scaling” · Zhenning Liu, Zhi-Yuan Wei, Michael Foss-Feig, Alexey V. Gorshkov, Andrew M. Childs

Figure

Empirical cumulative distribution of the optimality ratio (actual circuit error divided by minimum error among all 64 ordering patterns) for 4th- and 6th-order product formulas on 500 random 8-qubit chains. Unrestricted Karp optimization selects sequential circuits within 3.5% and 4.2% of optimal on average, while depth-3 Karp optimization selects wave-like circuits that strongly outperform fixed even-odd brickwall circuits.

Asks

How can term ordering be accounted for to accurately bound Trotter error and efficiently find the optimal gate sequence in product-formula simulations?

Before

Commutator-norm bounds overestimated 4th-order Trotter steps by 5–7× (Childs et al. 2021) and single-step errors by 1 order of magnitude at 2nd order and 3 orders at 4th order (Schubert & Mendl 2016).

But

Demonstrated primarily on 1D nearest-neighbor translation-invariant chains. Evaluates error for a specific step size τ rather than providing an analytic τp+1 scaling prefactor.

Tools

finite-window exact local dynamics · minimum-mean-weight cycle via Karp's algorithm · weighted de Bruijn graph · Suzuki-Trotter product formulas

Abstract

Product formulas are a basic tool for simulating quantum many-body dynamics, but a fundamental degree of freedom in their application---the ordering of Hamiltonian terms---has remained largely unexplored. Here we systematically study such ordering effects, quantifying their impact on simulation accuracy and exploiting them to design more accurate product-formula simulations. We develop an efficiently computable, ordering-sensitive bound on the finite-step-size Trotter error for geometrically local Hamiltonians for arbitrarily high-order product formulas. For translation-invariant one-dimensional chains, our bounds are close to exact second-, fourth-, and sixth-order Trotter errors in small-system tests, while on large-scale systems they improve on previous higher-order analytical bounds by orders of magnitude. We further use the local structure of the error bounds and estimates to optimize ordering efficiently, reducing the long-chain problem to a minimum-mean-weight-cycle problem on a weighted de Bruijn graph. For random translation-invariant chains, sequential (staircase-like) orderings consistently outperform standard brickwall circuits; when circuit depth is restricted, the optimizer instead favors wave-like parallel-sequential orderings, which preserve much of the accuracy advantage over brickwall circuits. These results establish ordering as a useful degree of freedom for both understanding and improving product-formula simulation.

We further use the local structure of the error bounds and estimates to optimize ordering efficiently, reducing the long-chain problem to a minimum-mean-weight-cycle problem on a weighted de Bruijn graph. For random translation-invariant chains, sequential (staircase-like) orderings consistently outperform standard brickwall circuits; when circuit depth is restricted, the optimizer instead favors wave-like parallel-sequential orderings, which preserve much of the accuracy advantage over brickwall circuits. These results establish ordering as a useful degree of freedom for both understanding and improving product-formula simulation.

item.title: A Basis-Aware Approach to Quantum Sampling of the Fermi-Hubbard Ladder
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Momentum-basis sampling reaches 0.47% relative energy error using 1.4% of the fixed particle-number sector at U/t=1, compared to 9.5% error using 33% of the sector in position basis under identical Krylov constructions.

Grade 0.357 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Adam Leicester, Zixu Wang, Jack Mandell, Yangyang Xu, Osama Muhammad Raisuddin, Haimeng Zhang, Jian Shi

Figure

Plots relative energy error |E−E0|/|E0| against retained subspace fraction for a 10-site Fermi-Hubbard ladder under position- and momentum-basis sampling across various interaction strengths U/t, Trotter step sizes Δt, and mixing layer counts L.

Asks

To what extent can one-body orbital basis rotations improve the sampling efficiency and ground-state compressibility of sample-based Krylov quantum diagonalization on the Fermi-Hubbard ladder?

Before

Position-basis sample-based quantum diagonalization (was 9.5% relative error at 33% sector size for U/t=1).

But

At intermediate coupling U/tleg=5 and isotropic hopping trung/tleg=1, compressibility remains poor, requiring k0.99∝3.106N/N states to capture 99% ground-state weight; hardware simulations face significant particle-number leakage at large sizes.

Tools

Sample-based Krylov quantum diagonalization (SKQD) · Density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) · IBM Quantum hardware (ibm_miami up to 120 qubits) · Fulqrum configuration recovery

Abstract

Sample-based quantum diagonalization can reduce the classical cost of many-body calculations by restricting diagonalization to configurations identified through quantum sampling, but its efficiency depends on how compactly the target state is represented in the sampled basis. We investigate this dependence for sample-based Krylov quantum diagonalization of the half-filled Fermi-Hubbard ladder using physically motivated one-body orbital rotations. Across position, momentum, bonding/antibonding, and leg-mode representations, the most compressible basis varies systematically with interaction strength and hopping anisotropy, with momentum sampling favored in the weakly interacting regime and geometry- or interaction-adapted representations becoming advantageous as the dominant energy scale changes. Near intermediate interaction and isotropic hopping, however, even the most favorable representation remains poorly compressible. Statevector SKQD calculations further show that basis choice strongly affects sampling efficiency. Hardware calculations on systems containing up to 120 qubits retain qualitative signatures of this basis dependence while revealing increasing particle-number leakage and reconstruction sensitivity with system size. These results show that scalable sample-based diagonalization requires co-design of the sampled representation, quantum circuit, and classical reconstruction procedure.

item.title: Two-body control of noiseless subsystems with mixed SU(3) representations lifts teleportation above the classical fidelity limit
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Adjacent exchanges and one singlet-projector interaction between fundamental and dual qutrits generate all special unitary gates independently across all noiseless subsystems for any r,s≥1. For four-qutrit encoded teleportation under correlated Weyl noise, logical fidelity exceeds the classical bound 1/2 while unencoded teleportation is entanglement breaking.

Grade 0.356 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Theory of Trotter Error with Commutator Scaling” · Otavio A. D. Molitor, Sergii Strelchuk, Michał Studziński

Figure

Teleportation fidelity plotted against transmission noise parameter. Identifies the noise interval where unencoded teleportation drops below the entanglement-breaking threshold while encoded teleportation stays above the classical fidelity bound of 1/2.

Asks

Can two-body symmetry-preserving interactions provide independent logical control across a mixed register of fundamental and dual qutrits without extra initialized ancillas?

Before

Fundamental-qutrit registers required three-body interactions for semi-universality, or two-body interactions using six ancillas (Hulse et al. 2021).

But

Pure and mixed tensor SU(3) collective noise only; gate sequence synthesis algorithm not provided; requires retaining trials where all 4 (or 5) qutrits arrive; diamond-norm perturbation bounds assume input-independent survival probabilities.

Tools

walled Brauer algebra · Lie-algebra control theory · mixed Schur-Weyl duality · correlated Weyl noise channel model · numerical pulse sequence optimization

Abstract

Collective noise can leave degrees of freedom unaffected, allowing them to store quantum information. Processing this information also requires physically available logical gates. We consider r fundamental qutrits transforming under U∈SU(3) and s dual qutrits transforming under its complex conjugate overlineU, with collective action R_(r,s)(U)=U^(⊗r)⊗overlineU^(⊗s). Using the image of the walled Brauer algebra and Lie-algebra arguments, we show that adjacent exchanges within each qutrit type and one singlet-projector interaction between the two types generate any independently chosen family of special unitary gates on the noiseless subsystems by a finite pulse sequence, for every r,s≥1. This establishes semi-universality of this system. We illustrate the result with a numerically optimised sequence of 24 pulses for three fundamental qutrits and one dual qutrit. We then use the encoding and available logical corrections for qutrit teleportation under correlated Weyl noise. Under explicit assumptions on channel composition and which trials are retained, and allowing for baseline implementation errors, we identify noise ranges in which encoded teleportation exceeds the classical fidelity bound of 1/2, while the unencoded teleportation channel is entanglement breaking. We analyse fidelity on accepted trials separately from the transmission costs of the additional physical qutrits.

item.title: Rate-Optimal Quantum Discrete Simulation Optimization
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Quantum discrete simulation optimization has minimax expected optimality gap Ω(|𝒳|/T), achieved up to logarithmic factors by the textscQUEST algorithm (O(|𝒳|log⁡T/T)). Convergence rate improves quadratically over budget T compared to classical bound Ω(|𝒳|/T), with worse scaling in decision count |𝒳|.

Grade 0.356 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Practical quantum advantage in quantum simulation” · Mingjie Hu, Jian-Qiang Hu

Figure

Expected optimality gap as a function of simulation budget T under Bernoulli outcomes with |𝒳|=20. Compares the faster decay of the quantum textscQUEST algorithm against the classical textscMC-EST baseline.

Asks

How does quantum computing affect the convergence rate of discrete simulation optimization in the fixed-budget setting, and can a provably rate-optimal algorithm be designed?

Before

Classical discrete simulation optimization has minimax expected optimality gap lower bound Ω(|𝒳|/T).

But

Fixed-budget setting with discrete candidate decisions |𝒳|. Continuous observation outputs require finite support discretization onto grid qubits.

Tools

sequential quantum phase-testing lower bound reduction · quantum Monte Carlo estimation · sequential elimination framework · slow-measurement mechanism · Qiskit numerical simulation

Abstract

Quantum computing has developed rapidly in recent years and has shown potential advantages over classical computing in various domains. In this paper, we study whether quantum computing can accelerate the convergence rate of discrete simulation optimization in the fixed-budget setting. We first formulate the quantum discrete simulation optimization problem by defining the quantum simulation oracle, the algorithmic performance measure, and the corresponding optimality guarantee. Based on this formulation, we establish a minimax lower bound on the expected optimality gap for any quantum algorithm. The lower bound analysis reduces the discrete simulation optimization problem to a sequential quantum phase-testing problem, and the resulting lower-bound argument may be of independent interest. By comparing the quantum lower bound with its classical counterpart, we show that the optimal convergence rate in the quantum setting exhibits a quadratic improvement in its dependence on the simulation budget, at the cost of a worse dependence on the number of decisions. We then propose the first fixed-budget quantum algorithm, called textscQUEST, for discrete simulation optimization. The algorithm combines a quantum Monte Carlo subroutine with a sequential elimination framework and uses a slow-measurement mechanism to help preserve quantum superposition during the optimization process. We prove that textscQUEST achieves the optimal convergence rate up to logarithmic factors. Numerical experiments further show that textscQUEST outperforms its classical counterpart, which provides empirical evidence for the quantum advantage in improving the convergence rate of discrete simulation optimization algorithms.
